sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Consensus algorithms are protocols that allow a set of distributed nodes to agree on a single value (or a single ordered sequence of values) despite crashes, network delays, and partitions; the dominant production protocols are **Paxos** (multi-decree, hard to implement), **Raft** (leader-based, designed for understandability), and **Zab** (ZooKeeper's atomic broadcast).

Consensus is the most fundamental problem in distributed computing: a set of nodes must agree on a single value — a log entry, a leader, a configuration change — even though some nodes may crash, the network may delay or reorder messages, and partitions may split the cluster. The problem is provably impossible to solve deterministically in an asynchronous network if even one node can fail (FLP impossibility, Fischer-Lynch-Paterson 1985), so real protocols make pragmatic compromises: they assume partial synchrony (network is usually timely, with bounded outliers), they use randomization to break ties (Paxos proposals with random backoff), and they accept that liveness may stall during a partition while safety is always preserved. The result is a family of protocols that are mathematically proven safe and practically available — Paxos, Raft, Zab, and their descendants — that underpin virtually every strongly-consistent distributed system in production today.

**Paxos**, introduced by Leslie Lamport in 1989 and formalized in 1998, is the original. A proposer broadcasts a numbered prepare request; acceptors promise not to accept proposals with smaller numbers; the proposer collects a majority of promises and then broadcasts an accept request with the chosen value; acceptors accept it if the number is still the highest they have promised. The protocol is famously hard to understand — Lamport's original paper used an extended metaphor about a Greek island parliament, and the multi-decree variant (Multi-Paxos) was left as an exercise for the reader for over a decade. Google's Spanner, Megastore, and Chubby all run Multi-Paxos internally. Paxos's power is its minimalism: it requires only majority quorums and monotonic proposal numbers, and it tolerates message loss, reordering, and any minority of node failures. Its weakness is implementation complexity — building a correct, performant Multi-Paxos is a multi-year engineering effort, and many production systems have shipped subtle bugs in their Paxos implementations.

**Raft**, published by Ongaro and Ousterhout in 2014, was designed explicitly for understandability. The protocol decomposes consensus into three sub-problems: leader election (nodes vote for a leader in a given term), log replication (the leader appends entries and replicates them to followers, committing when a majority ack), and safety (the leader's term and log indices ensure followers never silently diverge). The leader-based design means there is a single point of serialization per term, which simplifies reasoning at the cost of a brief unavailability during leader election (typically 100-300ms). Raft is now the consensus protocol of choice for new systems: etcd (the backbone of Kubernetes), Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV, and Redis Cluster's failover all run Raft. The protocol's clarity means a competent engineer can implement a basic Raft in a few hundred lines of code, and a hardened production implementation (like etcd's) is auditable line by line. The trade-off versus Paxos is that Raft is slightly less flexible — it commits to a strong leader per term — but in practice this is not a limitation.

**Zab** (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast) is the third major protocol, used by Apache ZooKeeper. It is similar to Raft in being leader-based, but it explicitly separates discovery, synchronization, and broadcast phases, and it provides a primary-order broadcast guarantee (a client sees its own writes in order). Zab is widely deployed because ZooKeeper is the configuration and coordination service for Kafka, HBase, Spark, and many others. Google's internal **Paxos-derived** protocols (MegaStore's Paxos group, Spanner's Paxos-per-shard) and Microsoft's **Paxos** variants round out the production ecosystem. The choice between these protocols rarely comes down to performance — they all have similar latency and throughput characteristics at the same replication factor — and almost always comes down to operational maturity, library availability, and team expertise.

The real-world impact of consensus is enormous. Every Kubernetes cluster's state lives in etcd (Raft); every Kafka cluster's metadata lives in a ZooKeeper quorum or the KRaft controller quorum (Raft); every CockroachDB transaction's commit goes through Raft; every Spanner transaction's commit goes through Paxos. The trade-off these systems accept is latency: a Raft commit on a 3-node cluster in a single region costs about 2-5ms (one round trip to the leader plus one round trip to a follower, both with fsync); cross-region Raft costs the cross-region round-trip time, typically 50-150ms, which is why multi-region strongly-consistent systems are rare and expensive. The architect's job is to identify what truly needs consensus — leader election, configuration changes, monotonic counters, transaction commits — and isolate it from the rest of the workload, which can ride on eventually-consistent replication. Consensus is the gold standard of correctness; the discipline is knowing when to pay for it.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant L as Leader (term=2)
    participant F1 as Follower 1
    participant F2 as Follower 2

    Note over L: Leader elected for term 2
    C->>L: propose(cmd=SET x=5)
    L->>L: append to log[3]=SET x=5
    L->>F1: AppendEntries(term=2, log[3], prevLogIdx=2)
    L->>F2: AppendEntries(term=2, log[3], prevLogIdx=2)
    F1-->>L: ack (log[3] appended, fsynced)
    F2-->>L: ack (log[3] appended, fsynced)
    Note over L: majority (2/3) acked -> commit log[3]
    L->>F1: AppendEntries(commitIdx=3)
    L->>F2: AppendEntries(commitIdx=3)
    L-->>C: success (committed)
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
         +-----+   propose(SET x=5)   +--------+
 client --|     |-------------------->| Leader |
         +-----+                      | (t=2)  |
                                      +--------+
        AppendEntries[3]                 |
        +----------------> +--------+    |
        |                  | Foll.1 |    |   AppendEntries[3]
        |     ack          +--------+    +----------------> +--------+
        |<-----------------                              |   | Foll.2 |
        |                       ack                      |   +--------+
        |<------------------------------------------------+
        |
   majority (2/3) acked -> leader commits log[3]
   broadcast commitIdx=3 to followers
   return success to client

   Term: 2   committed idx: 3   log: [noop, noop, SET y=1, SET x=5]
```

### Walkthrough
1. Client proposes `SET x=5` to the leader. Leader appends it as log entry 3, uncommitted.
2. Leader broadcasts `AppendEntries(term=2, log[3], prevLogIdx=2)` to both followers in parallel. Followers verify their log at index 2 matches the leader's, append entry 3, fsync, and ack.
3. Leader receives acks from a majority (itself + 1 follower, or both followers), commits entry 3, applies it to its state machine, broadcasts the new commit index, and returns success to the client.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
import random, time

class RaftNode:
    """Simplified Raft: leader election + log replication (single term)."""
    def __init__(self, name, peers):
        self.name = name
        self.peers = peers           # other node refs
        self.term = 0
        self.voted_for = None
        self.log = []                # list of (term, command)
        self.commit_index = -1
        self.role = "follower"
        self.leader = None

    def start_election(self):
        self.term += 1
        self.role = "candidate"
        self.voted_for = self.name
        votes = 1                    # vote for self
        print(f"[{self.name}] starts election term={self.term}")
        for p in self.peers:
            if p.request_vote(self.term, self.name, len(self.log) - 1):
                votes += 1
        if votes > (len(self.peers) + 1) // 2:    # majority
            self.role = "leader"
            self.leader = self.name
            print(f"[{self.name}] becomes LEADER (votes={votes})")
            return True
        self.role = "follower"
        print(f"[{self.name}] election FAILED (votes={votes})")
        return False

    def request_vote(self, term, candidate, last_log_idx):
        if term < self.term:
            return False
        if term > self.term:
            self.term = term
            self.voted_for = None
            self.role = "follower"
        # grant vote if we haven't voted this term and candidate's log is up-to-date
        my_last = len(self.log) - 1
        up_to_date = last_log_idx >= my_last
        if (self.voted_for is None or self.voted_for == candidate) and up_to_date:
            self.voted_for = candidate
            return True
        return False

    def propose(self, command):
        if self.role != "leader":
            print(f"[{self.name}] not leader, cannot propose")
            return False
        self.log.append((self.term, command))
        idx = len(self.log) - 1
        acks = 1                     # leader counts itself
        for p in self.peers:
            if p.append_entry(self.term, idx, command):
                acks += 1
        if acks > (len(self.peers) + 1) // 2:    # majority commit
            self.commit_index = idx
            print(f"[{self.name}] COMMIT log[{idx}]={command} (acks={acks})")
            for p in self.peers:
                p.commit_index = max(p.commit_index, idx)
            return True
        print(f"[{self.name}] proposal FAILED (acks={acks})")
        return False

    def append_entry(self, term, idx, command):
        if term < self.term:
            return False
        if term > self.term:
            self.term = term
            self.role = "follower"
            self.voted_for = None
        if idx >= len(self.log):
            self.log.append((term, command))
            print(f"[{self.name}] appended log[{idx}]={command}")
            return True
        return False                  # ignore duplicate

# 3-node Raft cluster
a, b, c = RaftNode("A", []), RaftNode("B", []), RaftNode("C", [])
a.peers, b.peers, c.peers = [b, c], [a, c], [a, b]
for n in (a, b, c):
    n.peers = [p for p in (a, b, c) if p is not n]

a.start_election()                    # A wins with majority
a.propose("SET x=1")
a.propose("SET y=2")
print(f"  final: A.log={a.log}, B.log={b.log}, C.log={c.log}")
print(f"  commit_index: A={a.commit_index} B={b.commit_index} C={c.commit_index}")
```

quiz.question: State the FLP impossibility result and explain why consensus protocols still work in practice.
options: When a new leader takes office, it may have followers whose logs diverge from its own — typically because the follower missed recent commits or has uncommitted entries…

The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) theorem proves that in a fully asynchronous distributed system (no bounds on message delay or relative processor speed), no…
quiz.explanation: The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) theorem proves that in a fully asynchronous distributed system (no bounds on message delay or relative processor speed), no deterministic consensus protocol can simultaneously guarantee safety (agreement and validity), liveness (termination), and fault tolerance (even one crash failure).

quiz.question: Compare Paxos, Raft, and Zab along the dimensions of leader model, log structure, and ease of implementation.
options: When a new leader takes office, it may have followers whose logs diverge from its own — typically because the follower missed recent commits or has uncommitted entries…
ZooKeeper uses Zab, which requires a leader and a quorum of 3 (out of 5) to commit writes.
Do not implement Paxos from scratch unless you have years of engineering capacity and a strong distributed-systems team.
Leader model: Paxos is technically leaderless (any proposer can propose), but Multi-Paxos in practice elects a stable leader (distinguished proposer) for performance;…
quiz.explanation: Leader model: Paxos is technically leaderless (any proposer can propose), but Multi-Paxos in practice elects a stable leader (distinguished proposer) for performance; Raft has an explicit strong leader per term, and all client writes flow through it; Zab also has an explicit leader (the "primary") and similarly centralizes writes. **Log structure: Paxos treats each log entry as an independent consensus instance…

quiz.question: What is a Raft term, and how does it prevent split-brain?
options: Split-vote elections happen when multiple followers time out simultaneously and become candidates in the same term, each receiving some votes but none reaching majority.
When a new leader takes office, it may have followers whose logs diverge from its own — typically because the follower missed recent commits or has uncommitted entries…
Single-decree Paxos agrees on one value: a proposer runs prepare-promise, then accept-accepted, and the value is chosen.
A Raft term is a monotonically increasing integer that serves as the protocol's logical clock.
quiz.explanation: A Raft term is a monotonically increasing integer that serves as the protocol's logical clock. Each term begins with an election: candidates increment the term, request votes, and the winner becomes leader for that term. Every message carries the sender's current term, and a node that receives a higher term immediately reverts to follower and updates its term.

quiz.question: Explain the Raft log reconciliation process when a follower's log diverges from the leader's.
options: Leader model: Paxos is technically leaderless (any proposer can propose), but Multi-Paxos in practice elects a stable leader (distinguished proposer) for performance;…
Do not implement Paxos from scratch unless you have years of engineering capacity and a strong distributed-systems team.
ZooKeeper uses Zab, which requires a leader and a quorum of 3 (out of 5) to commit writes.
When a new leader takes office, it may have followers whose logs diverge from its own — typically because the follower missed recent commits or has uncommitted entries…
quiz.explanation: When a new leader takes office, it may have followers whose logs diverge from its own — typically because the follower missed recent commits or has uncommitted entries from a stale leader. Raft's reconciliation uses the prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm fields in AppendEntries: the leader sends an entry with the index and term of the entry that should precede it; the follower checks if its log at that index has that term.

quiz.question: Why does Raft require fsync of the write-ahead log before acking, and what happens if you skip it?
options: Leader model: Paxos is technically leaderless (any proposer can propose), but Multi-Paxos in practice elects a stable leader (distinguished proposer) for performance;…
Single-decree Paxos agrees on one value: a proposer runs prepare-promise, then accept-accepted, and the value is chosen.
Consensus does not scale horizontally as a single group.
Raft's safety proof assumes that once a node acknowledges an AppendEntries, the entry is durable — it will survive a crash and be present when the node restarts.
quiz.explanation: Raft's safety proof assumes that once a node acknowledges an AppendEntries, the entry is durable — it will survive a crash and be present when the node restarts. This requires an fsync of the log file to disk before the ack; without it, the entry sits in the OS page cache and can be lost on power failure. Skipping fsync has two consequences.
